name: Lost in the Middle (Context-Position Awareness)
executive_summary: Models reliably attend most to information at the very start and very end of a long context and underuse the middle — place the most important content there, not buried in the middle.
description: An empirical finding rather than a prompting technique to 'apply': across long-context tasks, model performance on information placed in the middle of a long input is measurably worse than the same information placed at the start or end (a U-shaped performance curve). Directly informs how to place instructions, key facts, or retrieved passages within a long prompt.
when_to_use: Constructing any long-context prompt (long retrieved-passage sets, long documents, long few-shot blocks) — place the most critical content near the start or end.
when_not_to_use: Short prompts well within a length where position effects haven't been shown to matter.
known_pitfalls: This is a positioning heuristic, not a fix for context that's simply too long or too irrelevant — it doesn't substitute for good retrieval/filtering.

primary_source.authors: Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni, Liang
primary_source.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

variables.name: most_critical_instruction_or_fact
variables.description: The single most important piece of context, placed first

variables.name: secondary_supporting_context
variables.description: Lower-priority supporting material, placed in the middle

variables.name: most_critical_instruction_or_fact_restated
variables.description: Repeat the critical content near the end too, exploiting the end-of-context attention bump

usage_templates.reproducibility_note: A single LLM call (or a fixed sequence of them) with no external system dependency; running this template again at temperature 0 against the same model version should reproduce the same output.
